# Three ways to index a vector

Postgres can now index a `vector` column three ways: pgvector's **HNSW**, Timescale's **DiskANN**
from pgvectorscale, and **PRISM** from the newer pg_vectorsearch. The first two are graphs you walk,
the third is partitions you scan. The lab built all three on the same table and measured build
time, size, latency and recall.

## The contenders

**HNSW** (pgvector) is a layered proximity graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer and
descends, keeping `ef_search` candidates. There is no training pass, inserts are cheap, and `m`
(links per node) and `ef_construction` trade build time for recall.

**DiskANN** (pgvectorscale 0.9.1) is a single flat graph built to stay fast when it does not fit in
memory, with compressed vectors in the index (statistical binary quantization) and a rescore step
that re-reads full vectors for the best candidates.

**PRISM** (pg_vectorsearch 0.1.0, alpha, Postgres 18 only) is not a graph. k-means splits the table
into `nlist` partitions, IVF-style; each vector is stored as a RaBitQ code with an error bound; a
query scans the `prism.nprobe` nearest partitions and re-reads full vectors only for candidates the
bound cannot settle. It indexes pgvector's column in place:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON demo_docs USING prism (embedding vec32_cosine_ops);  -- build after loading
SET prism.nprobe = 40;                                               -- 0 = auto
SELECT * FROM prism_index_settings('demo_docs_embedding_idx');       -- what it chose, and why
```

## The measurement

20,000 random 64-dimensional unit vectors on Postgres 18, one laptop run, recall@10 against an exact
scan:

| index | build | size | best recall@10 | ms per query at best |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HNSW (m 16, ef_construction 64) | 2.7 s | 11.4 MB | 0.99 (ef_search 400) | 3.3 |
| DiskANN (defaults) | 20.3 s | 9.1 MB | 0.76 (search list 400, rescore 400) | 8.3 |
| PRISM (auto nlist 144) | 0.3 s | 1.8 MB | 0.98 (nprobe 160, every list) | 3.0 |

PRISM builds about nine times faster than HNSW here, at a sixth of its size, and nearly matches
its recall once every partition is probed. The automatic `nprobe` (10 here) reaches only
about 0.40, rising to 0.81 at 40 and 0.93 at 80.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read the test data, not just the table

Random vectors are the worst case for both quantization and partitioning: independent coordinates
leave nothing for binary codes to capture and no clusters for k-means to follow. That is why
DiskANN stalls at 0.76 and PRISM needs every partition. On real embeddings, which cluster
strongly, both do far better, and PRISM's automatic `nprobe` aims at about 0.95. Treat the table as
a comparison under stress, not a verdict.
:::

## Choosing

- **HNSW** is the default: no training, good recall at any size that fits in memory, mature.
- **DiskANN** when the index will not fit in RAM and you can afford the build.
- **PRISM** when build time and size matter (frequent rebuilds, many tables), on Postgres 18, and
  with the understanding that an alpha may need `DROP EXTENSION` and a rebuild between releases.

In SQLAlchemy all three are an `Index(...)` with `postgresql_using` and `postgresql_ops`; the queries
do not change.
